```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::knit_hooks$set(small_mar = function(before, options, envir) {
  if (before) par(mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 0.6, 0.6), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0))
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(small_mar = TRUE)

library(bbmle)

occ <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/bobwhite_occupancy.csv")
counts <- read.csv("../data/class_examples/bobwhite_counts.csv")

cutoff <- qchisq(0.95, df = 1) / 2

f3 <- function(x){ sprintf("%.3f", x) }    # three decimals, keeping trailing zeros

# one parameter: 52 of 71 routes in 2019
nll_2019 <- function(p){
  -dbinom(52, size = 71, prob = p, log = TRUE)
}
p_vec <- seq(0.55, 0.90, by = 0.001)
nll_vec <- nll_2019(p_vec)
best_2019 <- min(nll_vec)
ci_2019 <- range(p_vec[nll_vec <= best_2019 + cutoff])
p_hat <- 52 / 71
se_2019 <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / 71)
wald_2019 <- p_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se_2019

# a rare bird: 3 of 71
nll_rare <- function(p){
  -dbinom(3, size = 71, prob = p, log = TRUE)
}
p_rare <- seq(0.0005, 0.16, by = 0.0005)
nll_rare_vec <- nll_rare(p_rare)
ci_rare <- range(p_rare[nll_rare_vec <= min(nll_rare_vec) + cutoff])
p_hat_rare <- 3 / 71
se_rare <- sqrt(p_hat_rare * (1 - p_hat_rare) / 71)
wald_rare <- p_hat_rare + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se_rare

# two parameters: the logistic occupancy model from Thursday
occ_nll2 <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes, elapsed){
  p <- plogis(params[1] + params[2] * elapsed)
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
parnames(occ_nll2) <- c("a", "b")
occ_data <- list(n_occupied = occ$n_occupied, n_routes = occ$n_routes,
                 elapsed = occ$elapsed)
m_occ <- mle2(minuslogl = occ_nll2, start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05), data = occ_data)
a_hat <- coef(m_occ)["a"]
b_hat <- coef(m_occ)["b"]

b_vec <- seq(-0.10, -0.03, by = 0.005)
prof_fits <- lapply(b_vec, function(b){
  mle2(minuslogl = occ_nll2, start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05),
       fixed = list(b = b), data = occ_data)
})
prof_nll <- sapply(prof_fits, function(f){ f@min })
prof_a <- sapply(prof_fits, function(f){ coef(f)["a"] })
slice_nll <- sapply(b_vec, function(b){
  occ_nll2(c(a_hat, b), occ$n_occupied, occ$n_routes, occ$elapsed)
})

# fine versions for drawing and for the interval endpoints
b_fine <- seq(-0.10, -0.03, by = 0.0005)
prof_fine <- sapply(b_fine, function(b){
  mle2(minuslogl = occ_nll2, start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05),
       fixed = list(b = b), data = occ_data)@min
}) - m_occ@min
slice_fine <- sapply(b_fine, function(b){
  occ_nll2(c(a_hat, b), occ$n_occupied, occ$n_routes, occ$elapsed)
}) - m_occ@min
slice_ci <- range(b_fine[slice_fine <= cutoff])

ci_occ <- confint(m_occ)
ci_occ_quad <- confint(m_occ, method = "quad")
corr_ab <- cov2cor(vcov(m_occ))["a", "b"]

# a band around the occupancy curve, for the Lecture 21 preview
set.seed(21)
draws <- MASS::mvrnorm(2000, mu = coef(m_occ), Sigma = vcov(m_occ))
e_band <- seq(0, 22, length.out = 100)
curves <- apply(draws, 1, function(d){ plogis(d[1] + d[2] * e_band) })
band <- apply(curves, 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

# abundance against development
urban_nll2 <- function(params, y, u){
  mu <- params[1] * exp(params[2] * u)
  -sum(dnbinom(y, mu = mu, size = params[3], log = TRUE))
}
parnames(urban_nll2) <- c("mu0", "b", "size")
m_urban <- mle2(minuslogl = urban_nll2,
                start = c(mu0 = 12, b = -3, size = 1.4),
                data = list(y = counts$count, u = counts$frac_built),
                method = "L-BFGS-B",
                lower = c(mu0 = 0.1, b = -20, size = 0.05),
                upper = c(mu0 = 100, b = 20, size = 50))
ci_urban <- confint(m_urban)

# coverage: 100 imaginary 2019 surveys with the truth known
profile_ci <- function(k, n){
  ph <- k / n
  g <- function(p){
    -dbinom(k, n, p, log = TRUE) + dbinom(k, n, ph, log = TRUE) - cutoff
  }
  lo <- if (k == 0) { 0 } else { uniroot(g, c(1e-10, ph))$root }
  hi <- if (k == n) { 1 } else { uniroot(g, c(ph, 1 - 1e-10))$root }
  c(lo, hi)
}
set.seed(2026)
sim_k <- rbinom(100, size = 71, prob = 0.73)
sim_ci <- t(sapply(sim_k, profile_ci, n = 71))
sim_hit <- sim_ci[, 1] < 0.73 & sim_ci[, 2] > 0.73
set.seed(1)
long_k <- rbinom(10000, size = 71, prob = 0.73)
long_ci <- t(sapply(long_k, profile_ci, n = 71))
long_cover <- mean(long_ci[, 1] < 0.73 & long_ci[, 2] > 0.73)
```

# Two from the quiz

## Why the **negative**? {.smaller}

Same curve, same information. The only difference is the sign.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-width: 8.4
p_sign <- seq(0.02, 0.99, length.out = 400)
ll_sign <- dbinom(52, 71, p_sign, log = TRUE)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3.4, 3.6, 1.8, 0.6), mgp = c(2.2, 0.6, 0))

plot(p_sign, ll_sign, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#b2182b", ylim = c(-60, 5),
     xlab = "p", ylab = "log-likelihood", bty = "l")
arrows(0.45, -18, 0.08, -48, lwd = 2.5, col = "grey35", length = 0.12)
text(0.55, -10, "downhill", col = "grey35", cex = 1.0)
text(0.62, -40, "optimize() stops\nat p = 0.00007", col = "#b2182b", cex = 0.95)
mtext("no minus sign", side = 3, line = 0.4, cex = 1.1)

plot(p_sign, -ll_sign, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#1b7837", ylim = c(-5, 60),
     xlab = "p", ylab = "negative log-likelihood", bty = "l")
arrows(0.35, 30, 0.66, 6, lwd = 2.5, col = "grey35", length = 0.12)
text(0.26, 38, "downhill", col = "grey35", cex = 1.0)
points(0.7324, min(-ll_sign), pch = 16, cex = 1.8, col = "#1b7837")
text(0.72, 16, "p = 0.732", col = "#1b7837", cex = 0.95)
mtext("with the minus sign", side = 3, line = 0.4, cex = 1.1)
```

. . .

`optimize()` and `optim()` **walk downhill**. The minus is what puts the answer
we want at the bottom, where they are looking.

::: {.notes}
From the quiz: most of the class said the minus was about turning products into
sums, or about keeping the numbers from underflowing. Both true, both the log's
doing, neither the minus.

Draw the eye along the grey arrows. Left: downhill runs away from the peak and
off the edge of the plot, so an optimizer handed the plain log-likelihood walks
away from the answer. Right: the same curve flipped, and downhill now ends at
0.732.

The red curve is worth a sentence on its own. Its peak is at 0.732, in exactly
the same place as the green curve's bottom, which is the point: flipping the sign
moves nothing except which end the optimizer is hunting for.
:::

## What happens without it {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

52 of 71 routes held bobwhite in 2019. Leave the minus off:

```{r}
ll <- function(p){ dbinom(52, size = 71, prob = p, log = TRUE) }    # no minus

optimize(ll, interval = c(0, 1))$minimum
```

. . .

**p is essentially zero**: the fit says bobwhite are on none of the routes, when
they were on 52 of them. No error. No warning. Just a wrong answer.

. . .

```{r}
nll <- function(p){ -dbinom(52, size = 71, prob = p, log = TRUE) }  # minus

optimize(nll, interval = c(0, 1))$minimum
```

. . .

`optimize()` has a `maximum = TRUE`, so here you could go either way. **`optim()`
and `mle2()` do not.** They minimize, always, which is why we always write the
negative.

::: {.notes}
Run both out loud if there is time, or just read the output off the slide.

The lesson under the lesson is the one worth saying plainly: a sign error in a
likelihood does not crash. It returns a number, with the same confident
formatting as a right answer. Checking that a fitted parameter is somewhere near
what the data obviously say is not fussiness, it is the only thing standing
between them and a silent mistake. This comes back on Thursday with model
selection, where a wrong sign makes the worse model look better.

If someone asks why 0.00007 and not exactly 0: the optimizer stops when it stops
making progress, and at p that small the log-likelihood is already running off to
negative infinity.
:::

## A model is two things {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 8.4
p_of <- function(e){ plogis(a_hat + b_hat * e) }
e_line <- seq(0, 22, length.out = 200)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3.4, 3.6, 1.8, 0.6), mgp = c(2.2, 0.6, 0))

plot(occ$year, occ$n_occupied / occ$n_routes, pch = 16, col = "#4292c6", cex = 1.1,
     xlab = "year", ylab = "fraction of routes with bobwhite",
     ylim = c(0.52, 1), xlim = c(1996.5, 2022), bty = "l")
lines(1997 + e_line, p_of(e_line), lwd = 3, col = "#08519c")
mtext("the line: the average", side = 3, line = 0.4, cex = 1.1)

plot(occ$year, occ$n_occupied / occ$n_routes, pch = 16, col = "grey80", cex = 1.1,
     xlab = "year", ylab = "fraction of routes with bobwhite",
     ylim = c(0.52, 1), xlim = c(1996.5, 2022), bty = "l")
for (e in c(1, 11, 21)) {
  k <- 0:75
  d <- dbinom(k, 75, p_of(e))
  keep <- d > 4e-4
  xx <- 1997 + e + (2.8 / max(d)) * d[keep]
  yy <- k[keep] / 75
  segments(1997 + e, yy, xx, yy, col = "#d4b9da", lwd = 1.6)
  lines(xx, yy, col = "#762a83", lwd = 2)
  points(1997 + e, p_of(e), pch = 16, cex = 1.3, col = "#08519c")
}
lines(1997 + e_line, p_of(e_line), lwd = 3, col = "#08519c")
mtext("at each year, a whole distribution", side = 3, line = 0.4, cex = 1.1)
```

. . .

The **deterministic function** is the line: the average you expect in a given
year. The **distribution** is the purple shape standing on it: how far one real
survey lands from that average.

::: {.notes}
From the quiz: question 3 asked which of the two describes the average, and the
room split. The picture is the answer, and it is worth leaving up while they
look at it.

Walk the right panel one year at a time. In 2018 the line sits at 0.67. That is
not a prediction that 67% of routes will hold bobwhite; it is the center of a
distribution, and the purple shape says which other fractions are plausible. The
grey points are the years we actually got, one draw each.

Then connect the two panels: every grey point in the left panel came from a
purple shape like one of these, standing on the line at its own year. That is
the whole of chapters 3 and 4 in one picture, and the sentence to hang on to is
Bolker's: the function says what you expect, the distribution says how far from
it you land.

Why these shapes get narrower toward the top: the binomial has less room to
scatter as p approaches 1. Mention it only if asked.
:::

## Both halves are in the code you wrote {.smaller}

Thursday's occupancy model, with the two halves labeled:

```{r}
#| eval: false
occ_nll <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes, elapsed){

  p <- plogis(params[1] + params[2] * elapsed)   # the function: the average

  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied,                        # the distribution: the scatter
              size = n_routes,
              prob = p,
              log = TRUE))
}
```

::: {.notes}
This is the slide that makes the two previous ones stick, because it is their own
code from Thursday with nothing changed but the comments.

Every model for the rest of the semester has these two lines. The first one is
where chapter 3 lives, the second is where chapter 4 lives, and fitting is
chapter 6 asking which parameter values make the data most likely.
:::

# How sure are we?

## Where we are {.smaller}

| Section | Question | When |
|---|---|---|
| 6.1 - 6.2 | What parameter values make my data most likely? | Last Tuesday |
| 6.3 | What if the parameter depends on a covariate? | Last Thursday |
| **6.4 - 6.5** | **How sure am I about that parameter?** | **Today** |
| 6.6 | Which of two models is better? | This Thursday |

. . .

Same negative log-likelihood. **Today we read its shape**, not just its lowest
point.

::: {.notes}
The table they saw on Thursday, one row further down.

The sentence under it is the whole lecture in advance: a curve that rises steeply
from its minimum pins the parameter down; a curve that is nearly flat does not.
Everything else today is making that precise.
:::

## 6% a year, give or take what? {.smaller}

Thursday's occupancy fit gave $b = -0.062$: the odds that a route holds bobwhite
fall about **6% a year**.

. . .

Suppose the truth were 6% give or take 1%. Or give or take 10%.

. . .

| If the range is | Then |
|---|---|
| falling 5% to 7% a year | a clear, steady decline, worth acting on |
| anything from rising 4% to falling 16% | it might be **increasing**; we do not know |

**Same best guess. Opposite conclusions.** The range is what tells them apart.

::: {.notes}
Motivation before machinery, which is the order Bolker uses too.

Make it concrete for a manager: the first row justifies spending money on
bobwhite habitat; the second says go and collect more data first. A point
estimate with no interval cannot tell those apart, and that is why journals ask
for intervals.

Ask the room which one they think it is before going on. Most will guess the
first, because the decline was visible in the plot. They are right, and by the
end of class they will be able to say so with a number.
:::

## What is a confidence interval? {.smaller}

A **range of parameter values consistent with the data**, reported instead of a
single best guess.

. . .

You have seen them in polls: "48% support, **plus or minus 3 points**" is a
confidence interval of 45% to 51%.

. . .

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}
Three parts:

- the **estimate**, the best guess
- a **lower** and an **upper limit**
- a **confidence level**, usually 95%

**Narrow:** the data pin the value down. **Wide:** they don't.
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-width: 4.4
par(mar = c(3.6, 0.6, 0.6, 0.6), cex.axis = 1.2, cex.lab = 1.2)
plot(NA, xlim = c(-6, 18), ylim = c(0.4, 2.6), yaxt = "n", bty = "n",
     xlab = "yearly decline in the odds (%)", ylab = "")
abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey55")
text(0, 2.55, "no change", cex = 1.1, col = "grey40")
segments(c(5, -4), c(2, 1), c(7, 16), c(2, 1), lwd = 4,
         col = c("#762a83", "#1b7837"))
points(c(6, 6), c(2, 1), pch = 16, cex = 2, col = c("#762a83", "#1b7837"))
text(c(6, 6), c(2, 1) - 0.35, c("5% to 7%", "-4% to 16%"), cex = 1.2)
```
:::

::::

. . .

Today's question is where the two limits come from. Short answer: **they are the
values the data cannot rule out.**

::: {.notes}
A definition before any machinery, because "confidence interval" is a phrase
they have heard far more often than they have had it explained.

The figure is the previous slide's two scenarios, drawn the way they will see
intervals in papers: a dot for the estimate, a bar for the range. The dashed line
is zero, no change. The purple interval sits entirely to one side of it, so the
data rule out "no change"; the green one straddles it, so they do not. That
reading, "does the interval cross the no-effect line?", is the most common use of
a confidence interval in the literature, and it comes back at the end of today.

On the confidence level: keep it vague here on purpose. 95% describes how often
the method that builds intervals catches the true value, over many repeated
studies. It is not a 95% chance that this particular interval holds the truth.
That distinction is the "What 95% means" slide near the end, with a picture, which
is where it lands best. If someone asks now, say it is coming.

The poll is real-world framing only, and the margin of error there is the
plus-or-minus-1.96-standard-errors kind, which is the shortcut we meet later.
:::

## Start with one parameter {.smaller}

Back to the simplest version: **52 of the 71 routes** surveyed in 2019 held
bobwhite.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 7.4
plot(p_vec, nll_vec, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#762a83",
     xlab = "p, the probability a route holds bobwhite",
     ylab = "negative log-likelihood")
points(p_hat, best_2019, pch = 16, cex = 1.5, col = "red")
text(p_hat, best_2019 + 0.9, "best: 52 / 71 = 0.73", col = "red", cex = 0.85)
```

The best value is 0.73. **But 0.72 is barely worse. How far from the bottom is
too far?**

::: {.notes}
The curve from Lecture 15, deliberately. Nothing new on this slide except the
question.

Point at the bottom. 0.72 and 0.74 are almost exactly as likely as 0.73, so it
would be silly to claim we know it is 0.73 and not 0.72. Out at 0.55 the curve is
far higher, and those values really are implausible. Somewhere in between is a
line, and the question is where to draw it.
:::

## Get set up {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(bbmle)

occ <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/class_examples/bobwhite_occupancy.csv")
counts <- read.csv("https://github.com/bmaitner/biometry_course/raw/refs/heads/main/data/class_examples/bobwhite_counts.csv")

nll_2019 <- function(p){
  -dbinom(52, size = 71, prob = p, log = TRUE)
}

p_vec <- seq(0.55, 0.90, by = 0.001)    # candidate values of p
nll_vec <- nll_2019(p_vec)               # dbinom takes all of them at once

plot(p_vec, nll_vec, type = "l", xlab = "p", ylab = "negative log-likelihood")
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Two downloads, and both are the tables from data/class_examples, already built:
occ is Thursday's 23 rows, and counts is the 1,360 bobwhite route-years. Nobody
has to rebuild them with tapply this time, which is where Thursday's time went.

The last two lines are the curve on the previous slide. nll_2019 is only one
line, but it is worth reading it out: the data are fixed at 52 of 71, and p is the
thing being varied. That is what a likelihood is.

dbinom happily takes a vector of probabilities and returns a vector of answers,
so no loop is needed for a single parameter.
:::

## Drawing the line {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| fig-width: 7.4
plot(p_vec, nll_vec - best_2019, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#762a83",
     ylim = c(0, 8), xlab = "p",
     ylab = "NLL above the minimum")
abline(h = cutoff, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
rect(ci_2019[1], -1, ci_2019[2], cutoff, col = rgb(0.46, 0.16, 0.51, 0.15),
     border = NA)
text(0.87, cutoff + 0.45, "1.92", col = "grey30", cex = 0.9)
abline(v = ci_2019, col = "#762a83", lty = 3)
points(p_hat, 0, pch = 16, cex = 1.5, col = "red")
text(p_hat, 0.7, "best: 0.73", col = "red", cex = 0.85)
```

Keep every value of $p$ whose NLL is **within 1.92** of the minimum: the values
the data cannot rule out. That range is the **95% confidence interval**.

::: {.notes}
Same curve, shifted down so the minimum sits at zero. That is the only change,
and it makes the rule easy to read: anything under the dashed line is in.

The next slide says where 1.92 comes from. Give them the rule first and the
reason second, because the rule is what they will use and the reason is what
makes it trustworthy.
:::

## Where 1.92 comes from {.smaller}

Compare the best value with any other value $p_0$:

$$\text{deviance} = 2 \times \big(\text{NLL}(p_0) - \text{NLL}_{\text{best}}\big)$$

. . .

If $p_0$ **is the true value**, that deviance follows a known distribution: a
**chi-squared with 1 degree of freedom**. One degree of freedom because we fixed
one parameter.

. . .

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
qchisq(0.95, df = 1)       # deviance the true value exceeds only 5% of the time
qchisq(0.95, df = 1) / 2   # the same threshold, in NLL units
```
:::

. . .

Values within `r round(cutoff, 2)` cannot be ruled out. Values beyond it can, at
the 5% level. That is a **likelihood ratio test** run on every candidate value at
once.

::: {.notes}
The result is Wilks's theorem, and the book states it without proof, which is the
right call for this course too.

The doubling is a historical convention: the chi-squared describes twice the
difference, so we halve the threshold to compare with the NLL directly. 3.84 and
1.92 are the same rule written two ways, and they will see both in papers.

Callback to Thursday: the trend model beat the one-number model by 23 units, and
the notes promised a threshold of 1.92. This is that threshold. Thursday's
lecture on model comparison is the same test pointed at whole models instead of
single parameter values.

"Likelihood ratio" because a difference in log-likelihoods is the log of a ratio
of likelihoods.
:::

## Find the interval {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
best <- min(nll_vec)                  # the bottom of the curve

in_range <- nll_vec <= best + 1.92    # TRUE for every p within 1.92 of it

range(p_vec[in_range])                # the smallest and largest p that passed
```
:::

. . .

**Check:** you should get about **`r f3(ci_2019[1])` to
`r f3(ci_2019[2])`**.

. . .

Is the interval **symmetric** around 0.73?

::: {.notes}
Given in full: the logic is the point here, not the syntax. Read it from the
middle out. The comparison makes a TRUE or FALSE for every candidate p, the
square brackets keep the ones that were TRUE, which is the subsetting from
Lecture 7, and range() returns the two ends.

Symmetry: 0.732 minus 0.623 is 0.109 below, and 0.825 minus 0.732 is 0.093
above. It leans away from 1, because the curve gets steeper as p approaches 1:
there is less room up there, so the data rule values out faster. Remember the
asymmetry, because the shortcut on the next slide cannot produce it.
:::

## The shortcut, and when it breaks {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

The interval you have seen in every stats class: **estimate ± 1.96 standard errors**.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
p_hat <- 52 / 71
se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / 71)    # standard error of a proportion
p_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se
```
:::

. . .

| | from the curve | ± 1.96 SE |
|---|---|---|
| bobwhite, 52 of 71 | `r f3(ci_2019[1])` to `r f3(ci_2019[2])` | `r f3(wald_2019[1])` to `r f3(wald_2019[2])` |
| Eastern Wood-Pewee, 3 of 71 | `r f3(ci_rare[1])` to `r f3(ci_rare[2])` | **`r f3(wald_rare[1])`** to `r f3(wald_rare[2])` |

. . .

Change the 52 to 3 and try it. **A negative probability.**

::: {.notes}
The pewee is real: in 2019, Eastern Wood-Pewee turned up on exactly 3 of the 71
Florida routes.

For bobwhite the two methods nearly agree, and that is the usual case with plenty
of data and an estimate away from the edges. For a rare species, the shortcut
produces a lower limit below zero, which is not a cautious answer but an
impossible one.

Have them actually edit and rerun it. Seeing R print a negative number for a
probability is more persuasive than the table.

This is the same lesson as Thursday's straight line for occupancy: a method that
ignores the edges of the legal range works until the data sit near an edge.
:::

## Why the shortcut breaks {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| fig-width: 8.4
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3.4, 3.4, 1.8, 0.6), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0))
quad <- function(p, ph, se){ (p - ph)^2 / (2 * se^2) }
plot(p_vec, nll_vec - best_2019, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#762a83",
     ylim = c(0, 6), xlab = "p", ylab = "NLL above the minimum",
     main = "bobwhite, 52 of 71")
lines(p_vec, quad(p_vec, p_hat, se_2019), lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "#1b7837")
abline(h = cutoff, col = "grey70", lty = 3)
legend("top", c("the real curve", "the parabola ± SE assumes"),
       col = c("#762a83", "#1b7837"), lwd = c(3, 2), lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n",
       cex = 0.7)
p_wide <- seq(-0.03, 0.16, by = 0.0005)
plot(p_rare, nll_rare_vec - min(nll_rare_vec), type = "l", lwd = 3,
     col = "#762a83", ylim = c(0, 6), xlim = c(-0.03, 0.16), xlab = "p",
     ylab = "NLL above the minimum", main = "pewee, 3 of 71")
lines(p_wide, quad(p_wide, p_hat_rare, se_rare), lwd = 2, lty = 2,
      col = "#1b7837")
abline(v = 0, col = "grey40")
abline(h = cutoff, col = "grey70", lty = 3)
```

The standard error **pretends the curve is a parabola**. Symmetric, and blind to
the edge at zero.

::: {.notes}
This is Bolker 6.5, the quadratic approximation, and it is all they need from it.

A standard error comes from how sharply the curve bends at its very bottom. Bend
gives a parabola, and a parabola is symmetric and extends forever in both
directions. Where the real curve is close to a parabola, on the left, the two
intervals agree. Where it is not, on the right, they disagree, and the parabola
happily crosses zero.

The rule to give them: standard errors are a convenience. When they matter, or
when the estimate is near an edge, use the curve.
:::

## Two parameters {.center}

Thursday's occupancy curve has **two**: where it starts, $a$, and how fast it
falls, $b$.

How sure are we about $b$?

## Get set up, again {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Thursday's fit, with `mle2()`:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
occ_nll2 <- function(params, n_occupied, n_routes, elapsed){
  p <- plogis(params[1] + params[2] * elapsed)
  -sum(dbinom(n_occupied, size = n_routes, prob = p, log = TRUE))
}
parnames(occ_nll2) <- c("a", "b")

occ_data <- list(n_occupied = occ$n_occupied,
                 n_routes = occ$n_routes,
                 elapsed = occ$elapsed)

m_occ <- mle2(minuslogl = occ_nll2, start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05),
              data = occ_data)
coef(m_occ)
m_occ@min      # the lowest NLL it found
```
:::

**Check:** $a$ = `r f3(a_hat)`, $b$ = `r round(b_hat, 4)`, NLL
`r round(m_occ@min, 2)`, as on Thursday.

::: {.notes}
Same function as the end of Thursday. The one change is that the data list now
has a name, occ_data, because we are about to pass it to mle2 fifteen times.

m_occ@min: mle2 returns an S4 object, and the at sign pulls out one of its slots.
They do not need to know more than that this is the NLL at the best fit. It is
the same number as -logLik(m_occ), if they prefer that.
:::

## The surface {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-width: 7.4
a_grid <- seq(1.6, 2.45, length.out = 90)
b_grid <- seq(-0.10, -0.03, length.out = 90)
surf <- outer(b_grid, a_grid, Vectorize(function(b, a){
  occ_nll2(c(a, b), occ$n_occupied, occ$n_routes, occ$elapsed)
})) - m_occ@min
contour(b_grid, a_grid, surf, levels = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32),
        xlab = "b, the yearly change in log odds",
        ylab = "a, log odds in 1997", col = "grey55", labcex = 0.7)
points(b_hat, a_hat, pch = 16, col = "red", cex = 1.6)
```

A **tilted** valley. Correlation between the estimates: **`r round(corr_ab, 2)`**.

::: {.notes}
Compare with the negative binomial surface in Lecture 15, whose contours were
ellipses lined up with the axes. This one is tilted, and the tilt is the story of
the next few slides.

Why tilted, in biology: a curve that starts higher in 1997 has to fall faster to
pass through the same 2019 values. So a larger a goes with a more negative b, and
the data can trade one off against the other along the floor of the valley.
That trade-off is what a correlation of -0.89 means.

Contour labels are NLL above the minimum.
:::

## Slices and profiles {.smaller}

To ask about $b$ alone, walk across the surface along $b$. **What do we do with
$a$?**

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**A slice**

Hold $a$ at its best value. Compute the NLL.

Cheap. No optimizer.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**A profile**

At each $b$, **re-fit $a$**. Keep the best NLL.

One optimization per value of $b$.
:::

::::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-width: 7.4
contour(b_grid, a_grid, surf, levels = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32),
        xlab = "b", ylab = "a", col = "grey75", drawlabels = FALSE)
abline(h = a_hat, col = "#1b7837", lwd = 3)
lines(b_vec, prof_a, col = "#762a83", lwd = 3)
points(b_hat, a_hat, pch = 16, col = "red", cex = 1.4)
legend("topright", c("slice: a held fixed", "profile: a re-fitted"),
       col = c("#1b7837", "#762a83"), lwd = 3, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

::: {.notes}
Bolker draws exactly this picture in 6.4, and it is worth lingering on.

The slice walks straight across the valley, so it climbs out of it quickly. The
profile walks along the floor of the valley, because at every b it lets a move to
wherever is best. The profile is what we want: it asks "how plausible is this b,
if a is free to be whatever suits it?", which is the honest question when we do
not know a either.

Ask them to predict which will give the narrower interval before the next slides.
:::

## Your turn, part 1: the profile {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
b_vec <- seq(-0.10, -0.03, by = 0.005)
prof_nll <- numeric(length(b_vec))       # to hold the answers

for (i in seq_along(b_vec)) {
  fit_i <- mle2(minuslogl = occ_nll2,
                start = c(a = 2, b = -0.05),
                fixed = list(b = b_vec[i]),    # b held here; a is re-fitted
                data = occ_data)
  prof_nll[i] <- fit_i@min
}

plot(b_vec, prof_nll - m_occ@min, type = "b", ylim = c(0, 10),
     xlab = "b", ylab = "NLL above the minimum")
abline(h = 1.92, lty = 2)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Given in full, because the new part is the fixed argument and the loop structure,
not anything they have to work out. The next slide is the one they write.

fixed = list(b = ...) tells mle2 to leave b alone and optimize everything else,
which here is only a. With more parameters it would re-fit all the others, which
is why profiles are the thing that scales.

Fifteen fits; it takes a second or two.
:::

## Your turn, part 2: the slice {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Now the slice, on the **same plot**: hold $a$ at its best value instead of
re-fitting it.

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
a_hat <- coef(m_occ)["a"]
slice_nll <- numeric(length(b_vec))

for (i in seq_along(b_vec)) {
  # the NLL with a set to a_hat and b set to b_vec[i]
  # (no optimizer: nothing is being fitted. occ_nll2 wants
  #  a vector of both parameters, then the three data columns)
}

points(b_vec, slice_nll - m_occ@min, type = "b", col = "red")
```
:::

**Which curve gives the narrower interval? Why?**

::: {.notes}
Five to eight minutes. The missing line is

  slice_nll[i] <- occ_nll2(c(a_hat, b_vec[i]), occ$n_occupied,
                           occ$n_routes, occ$elapsed)

The common mistake is passing occ_data as a single argument. occ_nll2 takes the
three columns separately, which is what the hint is pointing at; mle2 unpacks the
list for them, but a direct call does not.

Several points of the slice fall off the top of the plot, which is part of the
answer: it rises much faster.
:::

## The slice is overconfident {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-width: 7.4
plot(b_fine, prof_fine, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "#762a83", ylim = c(0, 10),
     xlab = "b", ylab = "NLL above the minimum")
lines(b_fine, slice_fine, lwd = 3, col = "#1b7837")
abline(h = cutoff, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
legend("top", c("profile", "slice"), col = c("#762a83", "#1b7837"), lwd = 3,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.85, horiz = TRUE)
```

| | 95% interval for $b$ | width |
|---|---|---|
| slice | `r f3(slice_ci[1])` to `r f3(slice_ci[2])` | `r f3(diff(slice_ci))` |
| **profile** | **`r f3(ci_occ["b", 1])` to `r f3(ci_occ["b", 2])`** | **`r f3(diff(ci_occ["b", ]))`** |

The slice **pretends we know $a$ exactly**. We don't, so its interval is too
narrow by more than half.

::: {.notes}
This is the point of the whole two-parameter section. A slice is only honest when
the parameters are uncorrelated: when the valley runs along the axes, holding one
fixed costs nothing. Here the correlation is -0.89, and holding a fixed throws
away all the uncertainty that a and b share.

The profile is always at or below the slice, because it is allowed to optimize a
and the slice is not. A profile can never be worse than a slice through the
same point.

The general rule worth writing down: never report an interval from a slice.
:::

## The one-line version {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

`mle2` will build every profile for you:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
confint(m_occ)                    # profile intervals for every parameter
confint(m_occ, method = "quad")   # the ± 1.96 SE shortcut, for comparison
```
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  method = c("profile (`confint`)", "± 1.96 SE (`quad`)"),
  b_lower = round(c(ci_occ["b", 1], ci_occ_quad["b", 1]), 4),
  b_upper = round(c(ci_occ["b", 2], ci_occ_quad["b", 2]), 4)))
```

Nearly identical **here**: 1,730 route-surveys make the surface close to a
parabola. When they disagree, believe the profile.

::: {.notes}
confint on an mle2 fit profiles every parameter, the same thing their loop just
did, but with a smarter choice of b values and interpolation to find the exact
crossing of 1.92.

plot(profile(m_occ)) draws the profiles, but bbmle plots the signed square root of
the deviance rather than the NLL, so a perfect parabola becomes a straight-sided V.
Worth knowing if anyone tries it, not worth the class time.

summary(m_occ) also prints a standard error and a p-value for each parameter.
Those come from the parabola, so they inherit its weaknesses.
:::

## What the interval means {.smaller}

The interval is on the **log odds** scale. Back-transform the **endpoints**, as on
Thursday:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
exp(confint(m_occ)["b", ])        # yearly multiplier on the odds
```
:::

. . .

The odds of occupancy are multiplied by
**`r f3(exp(ci_occ["b", 1]))` to `r f3(exp(ci_occ["b", 2]))`** each
year.

So they fall by between **`r round(100 * (1 - exp(ci_occ["b", 2])), 1)`% and
`r round(100 * (1 - exp(ci_occ["b", 1])), 1)`% a year**, best guess
`r round(100 * (1 - exp(b_hat)), 1)`%.

. . .

**Zero is not in the interval for $b$.** So a flat line, $b = 0$, is ruled out at
the 5% level: an interval and a test are the same calculation.

::: {.notes}
Back to the slide that opened the section. The answer is the first row of that
table, not the second: a clear, steady decline. Say so explicitly, because it
closes the loop.

Transform the endpoints, never the standard error. exp() of an endpoint is an
endpoint; exp() of a standard error is meaningless. Note that the interval for
the percentage decline is slightly lopsided around 6%, because exp() bends it.

The link to the test: b = 0 sits far outside the interval, which is the same
statement as "the trend model beat the flat model by much more than 1.92 units".
Thursday makes that the main event.
:::

## How sure about development? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Thursday's abundance model, now with `mle2` so `confint()` works:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
urban_nll2 <- function(params, y, u){
  mu <- params[1] * exp(params[2] * u)
  -sum(dnbinom(y, mu = mu, size = params[3], log = TRUE))
}
parnames(urban_nll2) <- c("mu0", "b", "size")

m_urban <- mle2(minuslogl = urban_nll2,
                start = c(mu0 = 12, b = -3, size = 1.4),
                data = list(y = counts$count, u = counts$frac_built),
                method = "L-BFGS-B",
                lower = c(mu0 = 0.1, b = -20, size = 0.05),
                upper = c(mu0 = 100, b = 20, size = 50))

confint(m_urban)
```
:::

**Is zero inside the interval for `b`?**

::: {.notes}
Five minutes, mostly typing. Everything is given; the only question is reading
the output. Zero is far outside the interval for b, so the effect of development
is real, the same reading as the occupancy trend a few slides ago.

The bounds are named on purpose. Without names, mle2 warns that it is guessing
which bound belongs to which parameter. It guesses right here, but warnings that
are usually harmless are how real errors get ignored.

Answers on the next slide.
:::

## What it means {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  parameter = rownames(ci_urban),
  estimate = round(coef(m_urban), 3),
  lower = round(ci_urban[, 1], 3),
  upper = round(ci_urban[, 2], 3)), row.names = FALSE)
```

. . .

Bobwhite counts halve with every
**`r round(100 * log(2) / abs(ci_urban["b", 1]), 0)`% to
`r round(100 * log(2) / abs(ci_urban["b", 2]), 0)`%** of development. Thursday's
single answer was `r round(100 * log(2) / abs(coef(m_urban)["b"]), 0)`%.

::: {.notes}
The halving distances are b's two endpoints put through log(2) / |b|, the same
back-transforming as the occupancy slide. Shown rather than asked, to keep the
end of class light.

The intervals are narrow because there are 1,360 counts. Worth contrasting with
the pewee: data buy precision, which is Lecture 14's power analysis run in
reverse.
:::

## What "95%" means {.smaller}

Pretend we know the truth: $p = 0.73$. Survey 71 routes, 100 separate times, and
compute an interval each time.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.1
#| fig-width: 8
plot(NA, xlim = c(0.5, 0.95), ylim = c(1, 100), yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "p", ylab = "", bty = "n")
segments(sim_ci[, 1], 1:100, sim_ci[, 2], 1:100,
         col = ifelse(sim_hit, "grey70", "red"),
         lwd = ifelse(sim_hit, 1, 2.5))
abline(v = 0.73, lwd = 2)
mtext("the truth", side = 3, at = 0.73, line = -0.2, cex = 0.8)
```

**`r sum(!sim_hit)` of 100** miss. The **method** catches the truth about 95% of
the time. Any **one** interval either contains it or doesn't.

::: {.notes}
The figure that makes the definition stick, and the one slide worth slowing down
on.

Each horizontal line is one imaginary 2019, with its own 52-ish occupied routes
and its own interval. The red ones missed. Over 10,000 repetitions the coverage
is `r round(100 * long_cover, 1)`%, a little under 95% because counts come in
whole numbers; with continuous data it would be closer.

The trap to name: "there is a 95% chance the true p is between 0.62 and 0.83" is
not what a frequentist interval says. The truth is fixed; the interval is what
varies. The statement that sounds right is the Bayesian credible interval, which
is 6.4.2, optional.

In practice the two usually give similar numbers, and the distinction matters
more in exams than in field reports. But the figure is the honest picture.
:::

## From the parameters to the curve {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-width: 7.4
plot(occ$year, occ$n_occupied / occ$n_routes, pch = 16, col = "grey35",
     ylim = c(0.55, 1), xlab = "year", ylab = "fraction of routes with bobwhite",
     bty = "l")
polygon(c(1997 + e_band, rev(1997 + e_band)), c(band[1, ], rev(band[2, ])),
        col = rgb(0.46, 0.16, 0.51, 0.25), border = NA)
lines(1997 + e_band, plogis(a_hat + b_hat * e_band), lwd = 3, col = "#762a83")
legend("topright", c("fitted curve", "95% band"), lwd = c(3, 10),
       col = c("#762a83", rgb(0.46, 0.16, 0.51, 0.25)), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

The intervals on $a$ and $b$ become an interval on **the whole curve**. How to
draw it is **Lecture 21**.

::: {.notes}
A preview only: nothing to type, and no need to explain the method today.

What to point at: the band is narrowest in the middle of the data and flares at
both ends, the same way a lever wobbles most far from its pivot. Uncertainty in
the slope matters most where you are furthest from the center of the years.

Someone will notice that most of the points sit outside the band. That is
correct: the band is about where the average is, not where a single year's
survey lands. The scatter of individual years around the line is the binomial
from slide 9, and an interval that includes it, a prediction interval, is wider.
Lecture 21 draws both.

For reference, it was made by drawing 2,000 (a, b) pairs from the fitted
estimates and their covariance, computing the curve for each, and taking the
middle 95% at every year. That is the population prediction interval from
Bolker 7.5, which Lecture 21 builds by hand. Supplement 01 has a short version
under "The band, in six lines" for anyone who wants it sooner.
:::

## What you can now do {.smaller}

- Read an interval off a likelihood curve: everything **within 1.92** of the
  minimum
- Say where 1.92 comes from: half of `qchisq(0.95, 1)`
- Know when **± 1.96 SE** is fine, and when it gives impossible answers
- Build a **profile**, and know why a **slice** is overconfident
- `confint()` an `mle2` fit, and **back-transform the endpoints**

. . .

Still missing: **is the more complicated model worth it?** That is this
Thursday.

::: {.notes}
Point out that every interval today came from the same NLL function they already
had. Nothing about the model changed; only how we read it.
:::

## Additional practice {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Make the coverage plot yourself. Same ideas, less handholding:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# 1. one imaginary survey: 71 routes, true p of 0.73
k <- rbinom(1, size = 71, prob = 0.73)
# 2. its interval, by the method from earlier: an NLL curve over p_vec,
#    then the values within 1.92 of its minimum
# 3. wrap steps 1 and 2 in a loop that runs 100 times, saving each
#    interval's lower and upper ends in two vectors
# 4. what fraction of the 100 contain 0.73?
# 5. now set the truth to 0.03 instead, with 71 routes. Use the
#    +/- 1.96 SE shortcut. How often does it miss, and how?
```
:::

::: {.notes}
For outside class, or for anyone who finishes early.

Step 5 is the payoff: with a rare species, the standard-error interval misses far
more often than 5%, and it misses lopsidedly. It fails in exactly the situation
where people most need to know how sure they are, which is when the species is
rare.

The answer key has a complete version.
:::
